events.text: Kodak releases the Brownie, a box camera that sells for one dollar
The daguerreotype process is announced in Paris and given free to the world
Polaroid's first instant camera, the Model 95 Land Camera, goes on sale
The Lumière brothers hold their first paid public film screening in Paris

reveal.explanation: Photography went public in Paris in 1839, and within sixty years the same city saw pictures move when the Lumières sold tickets to a film show. The Brownie followed only five years after that screening and put a camera in ordinary hands, while Polaroid's instant prints had to wait until after the Second World War.

sources.excerpt: Invented by Louis Daguerre and introduced worldwide in 1839, the daguerreotype was almost completely superseded by 1856 with new, less expensive processes, such as ambrotype (collodion process), that yield more readily viewable images.
The Lumières gave their first paid public screening on 28 December 1895, at Salon Indien du Grand Café in Paris.
The Brownie was a series of camera models made by Eastman Kodak and first released in 1900.
The first commercially available model was the Model 95, which produced sepia-colored prints in about 1 minute. It was first sold to the public on November 26, 1948.
